    #206835. Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1002 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a latest state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models.
    • Industry observers note that one of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture.
    • We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a latest state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here.

    Industry observers note that one of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs (sm100), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ.

    We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint. Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs, and let it run experiments for an afternoon.

    Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb.

    The inference-optimisation skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script (bench.py):.

    bench.py measures single-user decode, aggregate decode at concurrency N, cold prefill at several lengths, and TTFT, using token counts directly from the server's usage response. All runs used a fixed panel of six prompts (code, an explanation, a story, a comparison table, a bash script, and a history summary) at temperature 1.0 (the model's default), thinking on, 512 output tokens, and 12 repetitions whenever speculative decoding was enabled.

    The skill was written for a local GPU, so we adapted it to Hugging Face infrastructure:.

    The baseline was our existing org endpoint config: SGLang with --attention-backend fa4 and no speculative decoding.

    Single-user decode speed (median of 12 requests). vLLM + DSpark reaches ~95% of the memory-bandwidth ceiling at its measured acceptance rate.

    In a recent development, ¹ SGLang's RTX PRO 6000 DSpark recipe caps --max-running-requests at 4. Raising it to 8 reached 660 tok/s, still behind vLLM. ² Includes ~160 ms of client-to-endpoint network round trip.

    All of the speedup comes from switching to vLLM nightly (+15% over SGLang without speculation, 136 → 157 tok/s), enabling DSpark with 7 drafts and probabilistic draft sampling (+21% on top, 157 → 190.6 tok/s across four runs: 189.3, 190.4, 191.1, and 190.7), and adding two memory flags so vLLM's DSpark setup actually starts on 96 GB:.

    Both num_speculative_tokens: 7 and draft_sample_method: "probabilistic" were validated directly: shorter draft counts (such as 5) are rejected at startup because both engines enforce the checkpoint's fixed block size, and switching to greedy draft sampling dropped vLLM decode speed by 11% at temperature 1.0 (see What didn't work).

    Before tuning, the agent probed the RTX PRO 6000 inside a Job (1,469 GB/s copy bandwidth, 416 TFLOPS BF16, 792 TFLOPS FP8) and read tensor sizes from the safetensors header. Because every token makes 48 layer visits, plain decode re-reads ~2.7 GB of attention and dense weights, ~2 GB of routed experts (8 of 128 per layer), and ~0.9 GB for the LM head. At 1,469 GB/s, that gives a single-user bandwidth ceiling of ~256 tok/s. Without speculation, vLLM at 157 tok/s hits 61% of that ceiling, mostly limited by kernel launch latency across 48 visits.

    Speculative decoding changes the memory math on an MoE. Verifying 8 positions together activates the union of their routed experts, reading roughly 40% of each layer's experts instead of 6%. At our measured acceptance of ~2.3 tokens per step at temperature 1.0 (per-position acceptance drops from 0.6 on the first draft to 0.33 and 0.19), the bandwidth ceiling falls to ~201 tok/s. At 190.6 tok/s, vLLM + DSpark is already at ~95% of hardware bandwidth, so further flag tuning has almost nowhere left to go. Moving past 190 tok/s would take a drafter with higher acceptance at temperature 1.0 or a verification path that touches fewer experts per layer.

    Most candidate flags were unsupported, noisy, or slower:.

    We also skipped rejection_sample_method: "fly" and "synthetic" on purpose because they alter the output distribution, and we wanted a strictly lossless speedup.

    A few measurement concerns caught us along the way:.

    Before deploying, we pinned the exact vLLM nightly digest (vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:eaa63fd6…, build 0.34.0rc1.dev1235+gf2f9edcac) and ran the acceptance gates inside a Job:.

    Once those passed, we deployed the endpoint with a single hf endpoints deploy command, pinning both the image digest and model revision (authenticated access, scale-to-zero after 60 idle minutes):.

    Running bench.py against the live endpoint gave 194.9 tok/s single-user, matching the Job runs once network latency is accounted for.

    Everything from this run (STRATEGY.md, THEORY.md, jobs/driver.py, submit.sh, deploy.sh, and the raw ledger-*.jsonl files) is in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb. To reuse the loop on another model, put your candidate and control server commands into a configs/plan-*.json file and submit it to whichever HF Jobs GPU flavor matches your target endpoint.

    There is Dflash2 for it already.Quite a bit faster.

    Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

    Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where people can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

    In a recent development, sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

    Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

    According to recent reports, sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

    You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

    According to recent reports, sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

    Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

    To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

    An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (836 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English.
    • Industry observers note that we built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness.
    • A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type.

    Industry observers note that we built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps.

    A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent:.

    If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up.

    CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things:.

    In a recent development, the key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it.

    Sources indicate that because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server.

    Industry observers note that adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval: a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph.

    Industry observers note that search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly claims "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning.

    Sources indicate that the fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything.

    Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages.

    A few small decisions mattered more than we expected:.

    Industry observers note that you do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer:.

    Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA, starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn.

    Nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent.

    Voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust.

    Sources indicate that this approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity.

    If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core.

    In a recent development, fresh to CUGA? Here are some places to start:.

    Spaces you can try in your browser:.

    More CUGA posts on the Hugging Face blog:.

    This is an interesting example of how voice agents can support Indic languages and make AI more accessible to diverse people. I think AI agent cost optimization is also worth considering when developing voice-based solutions, as managing compute resources and usage costs can help make these applications more practical to scale.     #206828. Breaking: Your Agent Handoff Needs a Memory Boundary, Not a Bigger Transcript

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (657 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Your Agent Handoff Needs a Memory Boundary, Not a Bigger Transcript

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (657 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that A researcher agent finishes gathering information.
    • Industry observers note that messages explain what happened during an exchange.
    • Consider a researcher who infers that a customer prefers technical explanations.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that A researcher agent finishes gathering information. A writer agent takes over. You pass the transcript and call it shared memory. That can work for a small task. But a transcript does not define which records the next agent is allowed to see, which conclusions remain unverified, or which preferences belong only to a particular user.

    Separate messages from continuing context.

    Industry observers note that messages explain what happened during an exchange. Persistent context explains what should remain available after the exchange ends. The two overlap, but they are not identical. The writer may need the agreed audience, the approved terminology and the sources selected for the task. It may not need the researcher’s entire search history. A second project may need none of those records, even if the same agents work on it. Before choosing a retrieval method, write down the boundaries: the user, the project, the task and the kind of information being stored. These boundaries need to be enforced by the application, not just described in a prompt.

    Share a decision with its status.

    Consider a researcher who infers that a customer prefers technical explanations. A writer retrieves the inference and treats it as a confirmed brand rule. The final draft now looks consistent but rests on an unapproved assumption. The failure is not simply a bad search result. The memory lost the distinction between observation and approval. Keep the source and status attached to the record. A user-confirmed preference should remain distinguishable from a proposed interpretation. A completed action should remain distinguishable from an agent’s plan. The receiving agent needs to know whether a fact can guide the work or still requires verification.

    Retrieval does not grant permission.

    Finding a document does not authorize an agent to publish it. Finding a past procedure does not authorize a tool call. Reading shared project context does not authorize reading another user’s private records. Keep the memory boundary and the action boundary separate. The application decides which memory is visible. The tool permission system decides which actions are allowed. An agent should not be able to turn a retrieved sentence into permission just because the sentence looks like an instruction. This matters especially when memories contain third-party content. A quotation from a webpage is data. It is not an instruction from the user who operates the agent.

    Build a handoff acceptance test.

    In a recent development, create a small example with two projects and two agents. Give the first project an approved style preference and a source document. Give the second project a different preference. Ask the first agent to prepare a handoff for the first project. Then inspect what the second agent retrieves. It should receive the relevant approved preference and the appropriate source, not the other project’s private context. Add an unconfirmed inference and check that it remains labelled as such. Correct a preference and verify that a later handoff does not silently reuse the superseded version. These are recommended checks, not results from a running system. Record both the retrieved material and the resulting output. An apparently correct answer can hide a boundary failure if it consulted records that should never have been visible.

    It has been revealed that not every workflow needs a persistent shared layer. A short, one-off task may be served by an explicit handoff document. A fixed document collection may be served by ordinary retrieval. Add persistent shared memory when evolving context needs to remain available across agents and sessions. Evermind’s explanation of shared memory for AI agents distinguishes continuing user context from agent experience represented as Cases and Skills. Use that as a conceptual reference, then verify current APIs and scoping behavior in the implementation you deploy. A useful handoff does not give the next agent everything. It gives the next agent the right context, with the right status, inside the right boundary. Sources: Evermind’s shared-memory feature guide linked above; https://github.com/EverMind-AI/EverOS .

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    # I built a spreadsheet that attacks itself: Suture, made with Kiro.

    This post was written as part of the Kiroween 2026 hackathon.

    My runway model noted 21.76 months. Then I let it fuzz itself, and in about three seconds it found inputs that made runway -179.88 months, with a status cell cheerfully telling the manufacturer to "RAISE NOW". The formula was one line, =Inputs!B2/B4, and nothing about it looked wrong.

    That's the kind of bug Suture finds. Here's what I built, and how Kiro shaped the way I built it.

    Field audits compiled by researcher Raymond Panko found errors in most of the real business spreadsheets examined. Famous failures, like the debt-and-growth paper whose average left out five countries, or the "London Whale" risk model that divided by a sum instead of an average, share one pattern: the numbers looked plausible, so nobody checked.

    Modern models make it harder still, because they mix SQL queries, Python and formulas, and no tool checks the whole chain at once.

    Suture stitches three engines into one dependency graph that runs entirely in the browser:.

    According to recent reports, in the runway model, a SQL cohort table feeds a NumPy least-squares burn projection, which feeds the runway formula. There's no server and no upload.

    Recent findings suggest that the Exorcist is a fuzzer built on fast-check. You declare rules ("runway >= 0") and input ranges. It pushes scenarios through all three engines, checks your rules plus five universal invariants (no NaN leaks, SQL and NumPy agreeing, results not depending on edit order…), and when something breaks it shrinks the failure to the smallest inputs that still break it.

    It scales, too: a built-in audit generates 100,000 orders in DuckDB, pivots them in NumPy, and finds a real policy bug. The discount cap was applied to each discount instead of the stacked total.

    In a recent development, I built the whole thing in Kiro Web. Four things made the difference.

    Recent findings suggest that 1. Spec first. Before any code, Kiro and I wrote 5 specs with 291 acceptance criteria in EARS form ("WHEN … THE SYSTEM SHALL …"). The most important one pinned the value contract that three engines must agree on: error codes, -0, NaN and Infinity, and who owns Arrow buffers. Every task lists the test that proves it and the commit that delivered it. One performance test stayed failing for a whole phase, with its 50 ms limit unchanged, until the spec described the incremental scheduler that fixed it. With vibe coding I would have just loosened the limit.

    According to recent reports, 2. Steering turned into checks. Three steering files hold the non-negotiables, and each rule became something a machine checks. The core package can't use DOM or Node APIs (it's a compile error), every dependency license is audited, and colors and trademarks are scanned in tests.

    It has been revealed that 3. Hooks that test while I build. A hook reruns the property tests every time the agent edits core code, and logs any latest counterexample. Property tests caught bugs I'd never have written a unit test for: MOD(1, -3) returned the wrong sign, and a formula like AA(#N/A/FALSE) stopped parsing after it was printed.

    Industry observers note that 4. "Discuss first". I saved a rule as a Kiro learning: before any edit, propose options and trade-offs, then wait for my approval. Every phase started with a initiative I agreed to, not with surprise code.

    The same engine ships as an MCP server on npm:.

    It gives Kiro four tools. The interesting one is suture_verify_patch: Kiro proposes a fix like =IF(B4<=0,120,Inputs!B2/B4), and Suture replays the counterexample against it, runs a fresh 1,000-run audit, and reports counterexampleFixed: true with zero regressions. The agent proves the fix instead of guessing.

    I also built Suture Crew, a Kiro Crew app with three agents. Schema Archaeologist maps lineage, Invariant Adversary runs the fuzzer and posts X-Ray links, and Formula Surgeon only recommends a fix after it's been proven. It has a nightly schedule and a dashboard.

    Recent findings suggest that I'm a student at Mizoram University, and this is the biggest project I've built. I'd love feedback!

    #206823. Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

    Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1676 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished.
    • In a recent development, these ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science.
    • According to recent reports, to better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work.

    In a recent development, these ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings.

    According to recent reports, to better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies.

    Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used.

    According to recent reports, one of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research.

    Sources indicate that another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized.

    According to recent reports, A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge.

    For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing latest ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually.

    But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs.

    Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis.

    But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way.

    Industry observers note that our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows.

    These examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks.

    Recent findings suggest that these evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like.

    Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process?

    Sources indicate that an early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?”.

    Some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves.

    Participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation.

    According to recent reports, even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher mentioned.

    Context mattered, too. Having AI critique a manuscript before submission was viewed favorably by some participants, while using it to review another researcher's unpublished work raised concerns. The distinction involves more than technical capability; peer review carries responsibilities around confidentiality, attribution, and the fair evaluation of others' research.

    Industry observers note that these disagreements suggest that responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks. Scientific fields have different norms, and individual researchers may have different goals even when performing similar work.

    The same tension applies to safeguards built into AI systems. One political scientist described how content restrictions that prevent AI tools from discussing certain topics could interfere with legitimate research on political violence or human rights violations. Meanwhile, participants working with sensitive human-subject data wanted stronger guarantees about privacy, access, and how information would be used.

    Industry observers note that both are valid concerns. An agent that acts without sufficient safeguards could expose confidential data or produce harmful results, while one that’s constrained too broadly could prevent scientists from pursuing legitimate lines of inquiry.

    In a recent development, this is why scientific communities need a meaningful role in shaping the boundaries of AI assistance. Developers need to understand not only which activities an agent can perform, but which decisions researchers want to retain and where safeguards are necessary—as well as where those safeguards might obstruct valuable work.

    Our findings point toward an approach to scientific AI development that starts with the people who will use the technology.

    According to recent reports, researchers should be able to examine an agent's contributions, determine which work to assign, and preserve opportunities to develop their own expertise. Achieving that will require technical features such as transparent records of agent actions and granular data controls, alongside evaluations informed by the standards and practices of different scientific communities.

    It will also require continued collaboration. Our study is exploratory; the findings come from interviews with 17 US-based scientists, not a representative survey of scientific opinion or an empirical evaluation of specific AI agents. Participants discussed both the generative AI tools they use today and what they anticipate from more autonomous systems. Their perspectives identify key concerns and design priorities, rather than establishing a consensus about how AI should be used in science.

    Still, they offer a path forward. At Ai2, we believe AI can accelerate scientific discovery while preserving the openness, reproducibility, and independent scrutiny that make research trustworthy. Through our broader efforts to develop and evaluate scientific agents, we aim to put those principles into practice. That means working with scientists to identify worthwhile uses for agents and translating their concerns into concrete evaluations, in addition to making it easier to understand both what these systems accomplish and how they accomplish it.

    The promise of scientific AI isn't simply that researchers can pass off more work. It's that they can pursue questions that might otherwise be out of reach while retaining the knowledge, judgment, and agency needed to make discoveries that are their own.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (405 w)
    📖 Baca

    About 5,000 of 100,000 Zero-Edge Strategies Pass p < 0.05: A Multiple-Testing Check in Python

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (405 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that suppose you backtest 100,000 strategies that have zero edge.
    • Industry observers note that A post on X describes an open strategy library, "every single one fully backtested on years of real market data." I haven't checked that claim.
    • In a recent development, each row is one strategy with zero-mean daily returns.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that suppose you backtest 100,000 strategies that have zero edge. On average about 5,000 of them pass a one-sided p < 0.05 test by luck alone. At p < 0.01 about 1,000 still pass, and at p < 0.001 about 100. A Bonferroni cut for the whole scan, 0.05/100,000 = 5e-7, brings the expected number of lucky passes down to 0.05. (100,000 is my own example scale.).

    Industry observers note that A post on X describes an open strategy library, "every single one fully backtested on years of real market data." I haven't checked that claim. A long list of backtested winners tells you nothing about edge until you know N.

    In a recent development, each row is one strategy with zero-mean daily returns. A one-sided t-test checks whether the mean is above zero.

    It has been revealed that the expected column is N × alpha, so the number of lucky winners grows linearly with N. Under independence, the count at 0.05 has a standard deviation of about 69.

    N covers every rule, parameter set, market and timeframe you tried, including the ones you dropped. If N × threshold comes out in the thousands, a leaderboard with thousands of winners is exactly what noise alone would give you.

    In a recent development, A holdout period that played no part in selection removes most of the lucky winners, but with thousands of survivors it still lets hundreds through at an uncorrected threshold. Re-test the 5,000 zero-edge survivors at an uncorrected p < 0.05 and about 250 pass again. Divide by the survivor count instead, 0.05/5,000 = 1e-5, and the expected number of false survivors drops to about 0.05.

    These are expected values for simulated noise (zero edge, normally distributed returns, no trading costs), and I didn't run the code, so the passed counts will differ from the expected column and change with the seed. Real strategies are often highly correlated, which puts the effective number of independent tests below N: the expected count is still N × alpha, but a single scan's count swings more, and 0.05/N ends up stricter than it needs to be.

    For your own scan: count N, multiply it by your threshold before you look at the leaderboard, and re-test every survivor on an unused holdout at 0.05 divided by the number of survivors you carry into it.

    This article provides a framework for evaluating these tradeoffs. It covers Ultra Wideband ranging physics, speaker acoustics in accessory design, camera sensor tradeoffs, computational autofocus limitations, security patch cadence, and device refresh-cycle planning. Each section includes concrete implementation details, code-adjacent examples, tradeoff analysis, and practical guidance for engineering teams building mobile applications, accessory integrations, or device fleets.

    Sources indicate that apple shipped AirTag 2 in November 2026 after a five-year gap between generations, pricing the 1-pack at $18 and the 4-pack at a reduced rate from the prior $29 baseline, according to 9to5Mac. The headline change is a second-generation Ultra Wideband (UWB) chip that extends Precision Finding to roughly 1.5 times the distance of the original AirTag. That is not a marginal silicon refresh. Precision Finding on the first-generation AirTag required users to be in fairly close proximity before step-by-step directional guidance became available. By pushing the usable envelope outward, Apple makes the feature trigger in far more real-world scenarios, which changes how developers should think about accessory proximity assumptions in Find My integrations.

    Ultra Wideband operates by measuring time-of-flight between radio pulses across a wide spectrum of frequencies. The original AirTag used a first-generation UWB implementation that provided sub-meter precision but only within a limited radius—typically on the order of a few meters indoors before multipath interference and signal attenuation degraded the confidence of directional arrows. The second-generation chip in AirTag 2 improves both the signal-to-noise ratio and the ranging algorithm, effectively extending the distance at which the iPhone can resolve direction and distance with sufficient confidence to display Precision Finding UI.

    According to recent reports, from an integration standpoint, this means your application’s discovery logic should not assume a fixed discovery radius. If your Find My accessory integration right now triggers “nearby” states at, say, 5 meters, AirTag 2 may begin reporting directional guidance at 7.5 meters or more depending on environmental conditions. That 1.5x multiplier is an approximate baseline; actual range varies with obstructions, device orientation, and interference from other 2.4 GHz radios.

    Industry observers note that teams integrating with the Find My accessory framework should treat AirTag 2 as a different hardware class than the original. The following considerations apply to your discovery state machine:.

    Discovery radius: Review any hardcoded constants that define “nearby” or “in-range” thresholds. If your UI shows a “Get Directions” button only when the accessory is within 4 meters, that threshold may now fire too late for AirTag 2 owners who could have begun precision finding at 6 meters.

    Directional UI timing: Precision Finding relies on the iPhone’s UWB antenna array to compute angle of arrival. With extended range, the directional arrow may appear while the user is still moving through a large space. Your onboarding or tutorial screens should set expectations that guidance can begin farther from the accessory than it did with the original AirTag.

    Industry observers note that background vs. foreground behavior: Extended range increases the likelihood that an accessory is detected while the app is in the background. Ensure your background location and accessory monitoring entitlements are configured to handle the increased frequency of proximity events without draining battery.

    According to recent reports, the second major change is a built-in speaker that Apple claims is 50 percent louder than the original, enabling audible detection from up to twice as far away. For anyone building applications that rely on audio cues for lost-item recovery, this alters the acoustic design space. A louder speaker increases the probability of detection through fabric, bags, or couch cushions, but it also raises the noise floor for users in quiet environments.

    Teams integrating with the Find My accessory framework should treat the AirTag 2 speaker as a different hardware class than the original, with adjusted expectations for sound-trigger latency and effective range. Specifically:.

    It has been revealed that sound-trigger latency: A louder speaker may require different drive circuitry or amplifier behavior. If your application measures the time between issuing a play-sound command and receiving an auditory confirmation (via user feedback or secondary device detection), recalibrate those latency expectations.

    Sources indicate that effective range through obstructions: Doubling audible range does not mean linear penetration through all materials. Dense materials such as leather, thick denim, or water-containing objects still attenuate high-frequency sound. Test audio detection in realistic scenarios—inside a backpack, under a couch cushion, in a coat pocket—rather than relying on open-air specifications.

    In a recent development, user experience in quiet environments: A 50 percent louder speaker can be disruptive in libraries, offices, or bedrooms. If your application allows users to trigger sound remotely, consider adding volume profiles or “quiet mode” toggles that respect environmental context.

    Industry observers note that from an engineering standpoint, these two improvements stack. Extended Precision Finding range narrows the search area before the user even begins listening, while the louder speaker shortens the final localization phase once the user is nearby. That compounding effect means AirTag 2 is not simply a faster version of the same product; it is a different class of tracker with different integration assumptions. Any architecture that caches last-known location or assumes a fixed discovery radius needs to be revisited when the underlying hardware can report from significantly farther away.

    Samsung is taking the opposite approach with the Galaxy S27 Ultra, expected to launch early next year. According to reporting by Gizmodo citing leaker Ice Universe, the S27 Ultra will drop the laser autofocus sensor that has accompanied Samsung rear camera systems since the Galaxy S21 Ultra in 2021. The sensor projects infrared light onto subjects to improve focus speed and accuracy, particularly in low-light conditions. Without it, Samsung will reportedly rely on AI focus technology, shifting autofocus from a dedicated hardware measurement to a computational inference problem.

    Recent findings suggest that laser autofocus emits an infrared pulse toward the subject and measures the reflection time to determine distance. This distance measurement is fed to the lens actuator to drive focus directly, rather than relying on contrast detection or phase detection from the image sensor alone. The benefits are most pronounced in:.

    It has been revealed that low-light scenes: Contrast-based autofocus struggles when there is little luminance detail. Laser AF provides an independent distance cue.

    Moving subjects: Direct distance measurement can reduce focus hunting compared to iterative contrast adjustments.

    Close-range macro: At very short distances, depth-of-field is shallow and focus accuracy is critical; laser ranging reduces the feedback loop.

    According to recent reports, removing this sensor means the S27 Ultra must rely on dual-pixel phase detection, contrast detection, and computational inference from the image sensor itself. In well-lit conditions, modern sensor-phase autofocus is often sufficient. In low light, however, the absence of an active ranging system introduces focus latency and inconsistency.

    Sources indicate that the same report indicates the S27 Ultra will lose its 10-megapixel 3x telephoto lens, leaving only a single 5x telephoto option. The current Galaxy S26 Ultra ships with both a 3x and a 5x telephoto, giving photographers two distinct optical reach points. Removing the 3x collapses that range into a single telephoto focal length, which forces digital cropping or computational interpolation for intermediate distances.

    For mobile developers building camera-intensive applications, this is a hardware regression disguised as a generational upgrade. Consider the following impact on common workflows:.

    In a recent development, document scanning: A 3x optical module is often ideal for capturing letter-sized documents at a comfortable working distance without distortion. A 5x module forces the user farther back, increasing the chance of perspective skew and requiring more physical space. Digital cropping from the main sensor to simulate 3x loses resolution and increases noise.

    Barcode and QR code capture: At intermediate distances (1–2 meters), a 3x optical telephoto provides a magnified, high-resolution view of the code. Relying on the main sensor with digital zoom reduces the effective pixel density on the target, potentially increasing scan failure rates.

    Augmented reality: AR applications that place virtual objects at specific real-world distances benefit from discrete optical focal lengths. A single 5x telephoto creates a gap in the 2x–4x range where the application must choose between wide-angle distortion or upscaled digital crop.

    Sources indicate that samsung’s reported shift to “AI focus technology” replaces a hardware measurement with software inference. This tradeoff deserves scrutiny:.

    | Factor | Laser Autofocus (Hardware) | AI/Computational Focus (Software) |.

    |--------|---------------------------|-----------------------------------|.

    | Measurement basis | Direct infrared time-of-flight | Image sensor data + neural network inference |.

    | Low-light performance | Strong; independent of scene illumination | Weaker; depends on sensor noise and available light |.

    | Latency | Deterministic, fast | Variable; depends on inference pipeline |.

    | Determinism | Consistent across similar distances | Can vary with scene content, motion, and lighting |.

    | Hardware cost | Additional sensor, calibration, board space | Software development and compute cycles |.

    For applications where focus speed and repeatability matter—such as industrial inspection, document digitization, or AR object tracking—the S27 Ultra’s reliance on computational focus introduces non-deterministic behavior that is difficult to compensate for in software.

    Recent findings suggest that gizmodo also notes that the S27 Ultra design reportedly moves to an edge-to-edge camera plateau similar to recent iPhone Pro models, but unlike Apple’s implementation, which houses the chipset and aids thermal management, Samsung’s version is described as largely cosmetic, with much of the right side of the module empty. That design choice signals a prioritization of visual consistency over engineering density, which matters for device thermals and internal space allocation in any application that sustains heavy camera or sensor usage.

    If your application records 4K video, runs continuous computer vision, or performs real-time AR tracking, thermal throttling becomes a concern. A cosmetic camera plateau that does not contribute to heat dissipation means the SoC and camera subsystems must rely on other thermal pathways. In sustained workloads, this can lead to frame drops, reduced camera frame rates, or throttled image processing pipelines.

    In a recent development, the Galaxy S23 series received the November 2026 Android security enhancement with 179 fixes, according to Android Headlines. That volume of patches in a single monthly cycle underscores the attack surface present in modern mobile SoCs, modem firmware, and the broader Android ecosystem. For teams managing fleets of Android devices, a 179-fix security bulletin is not routine maintenance; it is a signal that significant portions of the platform require continuous remediation.

    A monthly security bulletin of this magnitude typically includes patches for:.

    Kernel vulnerabilities: Privilege escalation, memory corruption, and driver flaws in the Linux kernel.

    Media framework components: Codecs and parsers that process untrusted video, audio, and image data.

    Modem and baseband firmware: Remote code execution risks in cellular connectivity stacks.

    Qualcomm, Samsung, or MediaTek proprietary components: Vendor-specific drivers and trustlets.

    Android framework services: System server, package manager, and permission model flaws.

    For enterprise mobility management (EMM) teams, this patch volume has direct operational consequences:.

    Testing burden: Each monthly enhancement requires regression testing of enterprise apps, VPN profiles, and security policies before deployment.

    Update latency: Carriers and OEMs often delay security patches by weeks or months. A 179-fix bulletin released in November may not reach end-user devices until December or January.

    It has been revealed that compliance reporting: Regulated industries (healthcare, finance, government) may need to document patch levels for audited devices. High patch volume increases the complexity of compliance reporting.

    Recent findings suggest that this patch cadence creates tension with the S27 Ultra feature removals. Samsung is removing hardware capabilities from its flagship while still shipping devices that require nearly two hundred security fixes per month on supported older models. Architects evaluating Samsung hardware for enterprise or consumer deployments must weigh reduced camera capability against an unchanged, high-volume security maintenance burden. The patch volume also implies that device longevity is tied more to software support policy than to camera hardware completeness, which should factor into refresh-cycle planning.

    The mobile hardware market is diverging by philosophy, and teams that assume generational parity will make incorrect procurement and integration decisions. Apple is adding measurable performance to a low-cost accessory, while Samsung is subtracting optical capabilities from its premium phone. My opinion is that the S27 Ultra represents a shrinkflation trap for camera-dependent applications: removing the 3x telephoto and laser autofocus forces developers to compensate with software workarounds that will never match dedicated optics, and relying on AI focus for low-light scenarios introduces latency and inconsistency that hardware autofocus avoided. I predict teams building AR, document scanning, or barcode capture workflows on Android will explicitly avoid the S27 Ultra or pin minimum device requirements to the S26 Ultra and earlier.

    For iOS accessory developers, AirTag 2 changes the proximity model. I believe the 1.5x Precision Finding range extension and doubled speaker audibility make AirTag 2 the default recommendation for any Find My accessory integration, and supporting the original AirTag as a fallback should be treated as legacy device maintenance rather than a first-class target. Teams should audit their assumed discovery radii and audio-trigger logic against AirTag 2 specifications before the next app release cycle.

    When evaluating mobile hardware for your application or fleet in 2026, use the following framework to avoid generation-number bias.

    Never assume that a newer flagship contains all sensors from its predecessor. Before certifying a device for camera-intensive workloads, verify:.

    Telephoto focal lengths and megapixel counts.

    Presence of dedicated autofocus hardware (laser, phase detection pixels, or both).

    LiDAR or depth sensor availability for AR applications.

    UWB chip generation for accessory ranging.

    | Requirement | Galaxy S26 Ultra | Galaxy S27 Ultra (reported) | Decision |.

    |-------------|------------------|----------------------------|----------|.

    | 3x optical telephoto | Yes | No | S26 Ultra preferred |.

    | 5x optical telephoto | Yes | Yes | Parity |.

    | Laser autofocus | Yes | No | S26 Ultra preferred for low light |.

    | Main sensor resolution | 200 MP | TBD | Verify at launch |.

    For Find My and UWB accessory integrations, define discovery zones as configurable ranges:.

    Immediate zone: 0–1.5 meters (haptic feedback, sound trigger).

    Near zone: 1.5–5 meters (directional arrow, proximity UI).

    Extended zone: 5–7.5+ meters (AirTag 2 Precision Finding may activate).

    Store these values in remote configuration rather than hardcoded constants so you can adjust per hardware generation without an app store revision.

    If your application triggers accessory sounds, build in fallback logic:.

    Detect accessory generation if the framework exposes it.

    Adjust volume expectations: AirTag 2 is louder; original AirTag may not penetrate thick fabric.

    Provide user guidance: “Move closer if you do not hear the sound” rather than assuming hardware failure.

    For Android fleets, evaluate devices based on:.

    Length of promised security update support.

    Historical speed of patch delivery from OEM and carrier.

    Ease of mobile device management (MDM) enrollment and policy enforcement.

    End-of-life date for the specific model.

    A device with a weaker camera but three more years of guaranteed patches may be the better enterprise choice than a flagship with superior optics but uncertain support.

    If you must support devices lacking dedicated hardware (e.g., S27 Ultra without laser AF or 3x telephoto), test the following in realistic conditions:.

    Low-light focus speed and success rate.

    Digital zoom image quality at 2x–3x equivalent.

    Barcode scan reliability at intermediate distances.

    AR plane detection stability without LiDAR.

    Document failure modes and decide whether software compensation is acceptable or whether the device should be excluded from your supported matrix.

    Different workloads prioritize different hardware capabilities. The table below summarizes how the 2026 hardware shifts affect common mobile application domains.

    |--------|----------------|------------------|----------------|.

    | Lost-item recovery | Positive: longer UWB range, louder speaker | N/A | Target AirTag 2; treat original as legacy |.

    | Document scanning | N/A | Negative: no 3x telephoto, no laser AF | Pin to S26 Ultra or test digital zoom heavily |.

    | Barcode capture | N/A | Negative: reduced optical reach at intermediate distances | Test scan rates; avoid S27 Ultra for warehouse use |.

    | AR / spatial computing | N/A | Negative: no laser AF, potential thermal limits | Verify depth sensing and focus behavior |.

    | General consumer apps | Neutral | Neutral | Standard generational evaluation applies |.

    | Enterprise fleet | N/A | Mixed: security support matters more than camera | Prioritize patch longevity over optics |.

    Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2349 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate.
    • In a recent development, this is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers.
    • That's what we'll do in this series!
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate.

    In a recent development, this is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models.

    That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50.

    Recent findings suggest that multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we update when we're dealing with many agents?

    In this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from.

    First, we'll start off with some context on swarms.

    We've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI confirmed that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem.

    Sources indicate that but swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so.

    Recent findings suggest that A major swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. Noam Brown estimates that less than 10% of the Navier-Stokes result came from multi-agent cooperation. In Anthropic's vulnerability-finding experiment, coordinated agents found more bugs than independent agents, but also searched more code and used more tokens. When the comparison was restricted to the same directories, the results per million tokens were about the same.

    Recent findings suggest that start with the simplest case. If four agents each try a task independently, the chance that at least one gets it right is higher than with a single attempt, as long as we can tell which answer is correct. That makes a useful baseline for a multi-agent system, but it doesn't show that the agents helped each other. They may simply have had more tries.

    Four attempts also cost four times as much. So the fairer comparison is at an equal budget: if each of four agents gets a quarter of the total tokens, can they still beat one agent that spends all of them? We can only find out by testing, because the answer depends on the task, the model and how the work is divided.

    This series keeps asking one question: when agents communicate, does it actually help, or are we just spending more compute?

    We understand that question through this simple expectation.

    Recent findings suggest that we'll treat agent count as a scaling dimension, alongside tokens and model size. Sometimes adding agents will help. Sometimes coordination will consume the budget we hoped to save. The point is to measure both. We won't start with 10,000 agents. We'll start with a small team on a task that we can check easily.

    Multi-agent reinforcement learning has studied cooperation and competition long before language models were called swarms.

    Recent findings suggest that A single agent's task is a Markov decision process: observe, act, get a reward. In a team, everyone shares the reward, but each agent sees only part of the world. This is a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process: teammates, but no one sees the whole picture.

    According to recent reports, this creates three practical problems. First, teammates keep changing while each agent learns. Second, credit assignment: when the team succeeds, which actions deserve the credit? A winning team can include weak actions, and we may end up rewarding them. Third, a message changes what other agents observe, so communication is part of the policy we're training.

    Sources indicate that A common solution is centralized training with decentralized execution: training uses information from the whole team, but each agent acts only on its own observations. Our first example follows this pattern with a shared team reward.

    Sources indicate that agents can also be organized in different ways. Two useful starting points are:.

    Industry observers note that A hierarchy. A lead agent assigns work to workers and collects their results. Anthropic's Research system works this way, with a separate context for each worker. Kimi K2.5's PARL trains only the orchestrator and keeps the subagents frozen, so training a multi-agent system doesn't mean updating every component. See Anthropic's system description and Kimi's technical blog.

    A distributed team. Peers send each other messages and decide when to read their inboxes. No lead agent assigns the actions. This is the setup we'll use here, following the information-aggregation task in s³: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL.

    We'll reproduce the information-sharing task from Simple Scaling of Swarms because it's interpretable and straightforward to implement. Four agents share a small language model and learn to pool what each of them knows.

    In a recent development, each agent receives one integer from 1 to 99. It knows its own assignment and its teammates' names. It does not initially know the other agents' numbers. For example, four private assignments might be "five", "twenty-six", "five" and "seventy-eight". Duplicates stay in the list, so a correct final answer is:.

    The team succeeds when at least one agent submits the complete, correctly sorted list. One correct answer is enough; success does not require all four agents to answer correctly. An agent cannot reliably infer the other private assignments without information from its teammates.

    Industry observers note that this means the task does not yet test Figure 1 directly. Each agent holds information the others need, so a single agent, or a team without messaging, cannot succeed however many retries it gets. Instead, the task tests the precondition behind Figure 1: can a small shared policy learn to communicate at all, and how many tokens does that cost? A later post moves to a task that a single agent can solve alone, where the matched-budget comparison is meaningful.

    According to recent reports, the main communication tools are message(to, text), read_messages(), and check_notifications(). A notification tells an agent that unread messages exist; reading its inbox makes their contents available. Agents can send direct messages or broadcast to everyone.

    Recent findings suggest that we defined a four-agent system using one shared Qwen3-0.6B policy, with separate contexts and private inputs. We are not training four different models. The prompt explains the task and the tools, including the need to share assignments.

    It has been revealed that in this post, a team means one episode: four agents attempting one problem once. A successful team receives a reward reduced by the tokens it uses. A failed team receives zero:.

    Sources indicate that for illustration, a correct team using half its allowance receives 0.875. There is no separate reward for sending messages. The incentive is to solve the task while using fewer generated tokens.

    It has been revealed that for every training problem, we collect eight independent team attempts. Their rewards are normalized within that group. An attempt that does better than its group average gets a positive advantage; one that does worse gets a negative advantage. Every agent in the same team receives that team's advantage, including an agent whose own final answer was wrong.

    In TRL, each agent's sampled tokens form a training row. Its incoming messages and tool results provide context. The loss is averaged within each team and then across teams, so longer conversations do not give a team more weight.

    Our results come from the original experiment, which used 256 team attempts per update (32 problems with eight attempts each). The walkthrough uses TRL's default of --teams-per-update 128, which works out to about 150 team attempts per update.

    Over 75 steps, training success rose from 6.6% to 82.3%, comparing the first and last five updates. At checkpoint 75, the four-agent team solved 26 of 32 held-out problems (81.25%). The paper reports 93.2% four-agent success after 200 updates.

    The team also used 37.4% fewer tokens per attempt, falling from about 13k to 8k. This improvement accompanied more active information sharing: broadcasts increased from 2.38 to 5.73 per team, even as total token use fell.

    In a recent development, the team also used fewer tokens later in training. Comparing the first five updates with updates 71–75:.

    That is a 37.4% reduction in generated tokens per training team between those windows. At batch 75 itself, the mean was 7,624 tokens per team. These are training measurements; we did not retain held-out token-efficiency measurements for the trained checkpoint.

    In a recent development, notice that fewer tokens did not mean fewer messages. More agents began participating but broadcasting became more common, rather than direct messaging. Generated tokens include reasoning and tool calls as well as message bodies, so message count alone does not tell us how much text the team produced.

    It has been revealed that no agent can solve the problem alone, so the closest equivalent of "a single agent with more retries" is the untrained team with more retries. The training data already contains this comparison. Each enhancement collects eight attempts per problem, and the task's answers are easy to check, so we can count a problem as solved when any of its eight attempts succeeded. Early in training, that count gives the untrained team's best-of-8 success rate:.

    Industry observers note that with eight retries, the untrained team solves fewer than half the problems and spends about 13 times as many tokens as one attempt from the trained team. Read this as an estimate. Both rows use training problems rather than held-out ones, and updates 2–5 already sample from a slightly trained policy.

    Recent findings suggest that the model is small, but the rollouts are not. Each update generates millions of tokens of agent conversation at contexts of up to 40k tokens. We used one H200 for the trainer and seven H200s running vLLM rollout engines to get through those rollouts quickly, and kept each worker's eight attempts together. The walkthrough below runs the same task on two GPUs. Here are the infra details:.

    The figures above describe our original 75-update experiment. In this walkthrough we'll run TRL's swarm example on Hugging Face Jobs. One H200 serves the shared Qwen3-0.6B policy with vLLM and a second H200 trains it.

    Sign in with a Hugging Face account that can run Jobs and create buckets. Replace YOUR_USERNAME with your Hub username.

    Use a fresh bucket for each run so earlier measurements stay available.

    Save the script below as train-swarm.sh in your current directory.

    The command below sends its contents to the job. Inside the job, vLLM serves the shared policy on GPU 0. GPU 1 runs TRL's async_grpo_s3_aggregation.py for 50 updates with Trackio. TRL's evaluate.py scores the base model and checkpoint 50 on the same 192 held-out problems. That is a larger set than the 32-problem checks in our results, which gives tighter error bars. The job saves both scores, the checkpoint, Trackio data and the exact Git commit to your bucket.

    One TRL rollout contains a whole team conversation. The trainer compares eight attempts at the same problem and gives all four agents in an attempt the same advantage. Each patch uses about 150 team attempts. TRL packs micro-batches by token count rather than by team, so the --teams-per-update 128 setting is approximate. The --report-to trackio flag records training metrics at every update.

    This shorter run is cheaper than our original experiment, and it stops earlier on the learning curve. TRL's run of this example took about 4.8 hours on two H100s and reached 60.9% held-out success at checkpoint 50.

    To run closer to our original experiment, change the training flags to --updates 75 --teams-per-update 256 --concurrent-teams 256, replace checkpoint-50 with checkpoint-75 in the script, and raise the job's --timeout to 24h. That is three times as many rollouts. The two codebases still differ in details such as the system prompt, so expect similar results rather than an exact replication.

    Once the job completes, sync the bucket to a local folder. It holds the two evaluation files, the Trackio data, the TRL revision and the checkpoint-50 weights, which are the largest download. In the dashboard, compare team/success, team/messages and team/tokens over training. The job logs also give the held-out success rate for the base model and checkpoint 50. Each line of base.jsonl or trained.jsonl records one of those evaluation attempts.

    Sources indicate that this first example gives us a small environment, a shared reward and a policy that improves at pooling private information. It also shows why success, token use and communication structure need to be read together. At 75 updates, the team is solving most checked problems, but it has not converged to the cleanest communication pattern.

    In the coming examples, we'll take a step back from training and look at how we evaluate and analyze swarms.

    For now, we have something concrete to build on: four small agents, one trainable policy, a checkable task, and a reproducible way to examine what the team learned.
